entries.title: Claude Drafts, People Decide
body: CS-Claude-Ops, my open set of Claude workflows for Customer Success, has one rule that shapes everything else in it: Claude drafts, scores, and flags. A person decides on escalations, pricing, and commitments.
It is worth explaining why that line sits where it does, because it is not a statement about what AI can't do. It is a statement about what a customer relationship is.
## What a customer relationship runs on

A customer renews because they believe two things: that the product delivers value, and that the people behind it will keep their word. The second belief is built one commitment at a time. "We'll have that fixed by Friday." "Your price won't change this year." "If response times slip, you get a credit."

Every one of those is a promise made by a person, on behalf of a company, and the company has to keep it. If a commitment gets made without anyone deciding to make it, the company is on the hook for something nobody agreed to. That is true whether the commitment came from an overeager new CSM or a model that wrote "we can do that" because it sounded helpful.
So the line is not "AI is bad at judgment." The line is that commitments need an owner, and the owner has to be someone who can be held to them.
## What Claude is good at in CS
Within that line, there is a lot of room. Most of a CSM's week is not spent making commitments. It is spent assembling information so that they can.
Gathering and summarizing. Pulling usage, tickets, notes, and contract terms into one view of an account. The account review and handoff packet prompts do this.

Applying rules consistently. Scoring every account the same way, every week, and flagging every band drop. People are inconsistent at this, and not because they are careless: they have 40 accounts and a calendar full of meetings.
Drafting. First versions of emails, QBR outlines, and internal updates, with the facts in place and the commitments marked for someone to approve.
Catching what slipped. An informal promise buried in a sales thread. An executive sponsor nobody has spoken to in 95 days. A renewal notice period about to pass.
Each of these makes the human decision better informed and faster. None of them makes the decision.
## How the line is enforced
Saying "people decide" is easy. Building it into the tools takes specific choices, and the prompts and specs in that repo try to make them:
Placeholders instead of promises. The customer email prompt writes [NEEDS APPROVAL: what and from whom] wherever a commitment would go. The draft cannot be sent as-is without someone resolving it.
Routing instead of recommending. The contract redline prompt says who needs to weigh in on each change. It does not say whether to accept it.
Evidence instead of verdicts. The competency evaluation gathers examples per area. A manager decides what they add up to.
Read by default, writes confirmed. The HubSpot agent interface lets an agent read freely, propose changes as a diff, and apply them only after a person confirms each batch.
The pattern is the same everywhere: the model does the work up to the point of decision, makes the decision easy to see, and stops.
## The cost of getting it wrong in the other direction

There is a failure mode on the other side, too. A team that trusts nothing the model produces will re-check every summary and rewrite every draft, and get none of the benefit. Worse, it will keep making decisions on the same incomplete information it always had.

The answer is not blanket trust or blanket suspicion. It is knowing which parts of the output to check. Every prompt in the repo ends with its known failure modes for that reason: they tell the reviewer where to look. A reviewer who knows that the renewal prep prompt tends to overstate thin outcomes can check the value story in two minutes, rather than re-doing the whole prep.
## Measuring it honestly

The same discipline applies to the business case. Time saved is real, but it is only worth money if it is used. Freed hours that turn into more accounts per CSM, or a hire you don't need to make, are savings. Freed hours that vanish into more meetings are not. The ROI calculator reports the cash return on its own for that reason.
A copilot pays for itself when it helps people make better decisions, sooner, about the accounts that matter. That is a high bar, and it is the right one.
Cross-posted from the essays folder in CS-Claude-Ops.

entries.title: Replacing Strong with something I actually own
body: I have been using the Strong app to track lifting for a while. It works, but I do not own the data in any meaningful way, and I wanted the ability to close the loop between logging a workout and getting recommendations for the next one.

Today I shipped that. LiftCycle is a Next.js app with a Supabase backend. You log your sets, and overnight an agent I have running analyzes the last two sessions per lift and applies linear progression rules. Open the app next session and your weights are already filled in.

The progression logic is simple on purpose: if you hit all reps cleanly two sessions in a row, add weight. If you missed reps, hold. If you have stalled three sessions at the same weight, flag it. No percentages, no periodization charts, just a system that keeps moving forward until it cannot.

The part I am most happy about is that I own all of it. The app is mine, the database is mine, the progression script runs on my own infrastructure. No subscription, no vendor lock-in, no dark patterns nudging me toward a premium tier.

I also started a paper trading bot for BTC/USD today. DCA plus momentum signals using a 20-period SMA and RSI. One hundred dollars of virtual capital, running hourly. Checking back in a week to see if the strategy is worth putting real money behind.
Two different projects, same underlying idea: automate the boring part so you can focus on the part that actually requires you.

entries.title: Why this journal exists
body: I want this space to feel more like a workbench than a portfolio.
This is where I capture what I am building, what I am learning, and where I get stuck.
The goal is consistency, not polish.

entries.title: forHumanity reached operational baseline
body: Shipped CI, hardening, observability, backup/recovery, and launch checklists.
The biggest shift: this stopped being just code and became an operable system.
Next question is user adoption and real-world feedback loops.

entries.title: What I want to explore next
body: I am interested in building practical AI operators that help run projects end to end.
Not demos. Systems that can deploy, monitor, and recover.
This journal is where those experiments will be tracked.

entries.title: AI, uncertainty, and what it means to stay human
body: I often think about the impact AI will have on life, society, work, everything, and truth.
It feels unavoidable. Everywhere you look, there is an article about the positives and the negatives.
Just this past weekend, there was a piece in the NY Times about an 85-year-old woman whose quality of life improved after getting a companion robot.

At the same time, there was an opinion piece mourning the loss of human connection and pointing out that even the people building large language systems do not really know what will happen or where this all goes.
I cannot help feeling like this is how evolution works. There are no certainties. No guarantees.
We cannot know everything, and we cannot control everything yet. Still, we try, and that tension is fascinating.
As humans, we want to control as much as possible while innovating as fast as possible in ways that are inherently uncontrollable.
I understand the fear and uncertainty.
I do find it concerning when people choose a chatbot or avatar over real human connection.
To me, that reflects a deeper societal failure, that people have become so isolated that those outlets are the only way they feel heard and seen.
At the same time, I believe AI can help us advance and explore what it really means to be human, and what humanity is, beyond productivity gains, faster output, or corporate enrichment.
The real question is: How do we evolve as humanity while developing and bringing this potential new life form into existence?
That is the question I look forward to thinking about as we move forward.
